client: I’ve been feeling really anxious about the family reunion coming up next month. Ever since the argument I had with my cousin last year, I can’t stop thinking about how awkward it’s going to be. My heart starts racing just imagining being in the same room with them, and I’m not sure if therapy can really help me deal with this.
therapist: It sounds like this upcoming reunion is bringing up a lot of difficult emotions for you, especially after what happened with your cousin last year. That racing heart and sense of dread shows how real this anxiety feels for you. What thoughts tend to go through your mind when you picture being in that room together?

client: I keep thinking about how uncomfortable it’s going to be, and I’m worried they might bring up the argument again or that everyone else will judge me for it. I feel like I’ll freeze up and not know what to say, and it’ll just make things worse. Honestly, I don’t know if there’s even a way to fix this—it feels like the damage is already done.
therapist: Your mind is predicting the worst-case scenario, which makes complete sense given how painful that argument was. Let's gently examine whether there might be other possible outcomes between "everything is ruined" and "everything is perfect." What's one small way you could prepare yourself for this reunion that feels manageable?

client: I guess I could try reaching out to my cousin beforehand to test the waters, but that terrifies me because what if they ignore me or say something hurtful? It feels like opening myself up to rejection all over again. Maybe it's better to just avoid them at the reunion completely.
therapist: It’s completely understandable to feel terrified about reaching out, especially when there’s a fear of rejection or more hurtful words. Avoiding them might feel safer in the short term, but it could also leave you feeling more isolated in the long run. What would it feel like to prepare for both possibilities—that they might respond positively or negatively—so you’re not caught off guard?

client: I never really thought about preparing for both outcomes - I've just been assuming the worst. But even if I did prepare, I'm not sure what I'd actually do differently. Part of me thinks no amount of preparation will stop me from panicking when I actually see them face-to-face.
therapist: It's so human to assume the worst—our minds often do that to try to protect us. Let's explore together what might help you feel just 10% more grounded in that moment, whether it's a breathing technique or a simple mental phrase. What's helped you cope with overwhelming moments in the past?

client: Sometimes counting to ten helps when I'm really anxious, but at family stuff it feels different because I can't just step away and do that. People notice. And honestly, when things got bad with my cousin last time, no breathing trick stopped me from feeling completely humiliated. That's why I don't trust that stuff to work when it really matters.
therapist: It sounds like you’ve tried grounding techniques before, but they didn’t feel powerful enough in the moment, especially when emotions were so intense and others were watching. That sense of humiliation from last time must have made it even harder to feel in control. What would it feel like to plan a small, subtle way to ground yourself—like focusing on your feet or quietly noticing three things around you—that doesn’t require stepping away?

client: Focusing on my feet or surroundings might be less obvious, but I worry it'll just distract me for a second before the anxiety comes crashing back. What if I try that and still end up feeling just as overwhelmed? It's like putting a tiny bandaid on a gaping wound. I don't want to look stupid standing there staring at my shoes while my cousin glares at me.
therapist: It makes sense to feel skeptical about whether small strategies like this could make a difference when the pain feels so big—like a bandaid on a wound, as you said. Let’s think of this as one tool in a toolbox, not the only solution, and explore what else might help you feel more prepared. What’s one thing you could say to yourself, even silently, if you started to feel overwhelmed in that moment?

client: Maybe I could tell myself "This is temporary, you've survived awkward moments before," but part of me thinks that's just lying to myself. The truth is some family wounds don't heal, and this might always feel awful. I don't want to pretend things are fine when they're not.
therapist: You're absolutely right—we can't force positivity when the hurt runs deep, and pretending things are fine often makes them feel worse. Your honesty about how much this still stings is important to acknowledge. Instead of pushing for the pain to disappear, what would it look like to honor these feelings while also giving yourself permission to find moments of ease, however small?

client: I guess I could try to let myself feel the hurt without beating myself up for it, but that seems impossible when I'm around my family. They always expect everyone to act happy, so any sadness or discomfort just makes things worse. I don't know how to honor my feelings when the whole environment feels like it's working against me.
therapist: It sounds like your family’s expectation to always appear happy adds an extra layer of pressure, making it even harder to acknowledge your own feelings. That’s such a heavy burden to carry on top of everything else. What would it feel like to give yourself permission to feel whatever comes up, even if just internally, without worrying about whether it matches the family’s expectations?

client: I don't know if I can separate my feelings from their expectations - they're so intertwined. When I try to give myself permission to feel bad, I just hear my mom's voice saying "Don't ruin the mood for everyone." Maybe that's why I freeze up, because I'm constantly policing my own reactions.
therapist: It makes so much sense that you freeze when caught between honoring your true feelings and fearing you'll "ruin the mood"—that policing must be exhausting. That critical inner voice from your mom shows how deeply these expectations have shaped your reactions. What would it feel like to notice that voice without letting it dictate your choices in the moment?

client: Noticing the voice is one thing, but actually not letting it control me seems impossible. That voice feels like part of me now - when it says "don't ruin things," my whole body tenses up automatically. I don't know how to separate from something that's been drilled into me since childhood.
therapist: That automatic tension in your body shows how deeply wired this response is—it's not just thoughts, but a whole physical reaction that kicks in instantly. These patterns that formed over years can't be unwound quickly, and it's okay if this takes patient practice. What would it feel like to simply observe that tension next time, without judging whether it's good or bad?
